title: Locally run AI models could do 90pc of tasks for cheaper: inquiry
full_text:
Almost all of Australia's artificial intelligence tasks could be done by cheap, locally trained models only slightly less capable than frontier labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic, say tech leaders, but Australia is falling well behind on investing in local capability.
Appearing before a parliamentary inquiry into AI on Wednesday, Rupert Taylor Price, founder of cloud computing supplier Vault Cloud, said up to 90 per cent of tasks could be handled by simpler models that were cheaper and easier to build in Australia.
"The majority of [AI] work that an organisation needs is not the absolute smartest brain at all times. It's very inefficient to put the smartest brain in the organisation to manage the diary and things like that," Taylor Price said.
Nexrupta founder Dan Navfield said frontier models were best suited to solving world-changing problems and deep research such as finding a cancer cure.
"They absolutely make up part of the offering that we need to have available to Australia, but they make up a smaller portion than we are led to believe," he told the committee.
Fellow Nexrupta director Dale Senti said comparable models could be run a sixth of the price of frontier models.
Taylor Price, whose company received a $22.5 million investment from the Albanese government's signature $15 billion National Reconstruction Fund, said Australia was dwarfed by other countries when it came to investing in AI ecosystems.
"I'd feel bad for biting the hand that feeds me, and noting that we are a partly Commonwealth-owned entity through the National Reconstruction Fund ... but when you compare it to the scale [of investment] ... in other countries it's just not comparable," Taylor Price said.
"It's in millions and hundreds of millions when other countries are doing billions and hundreds of billions. It's orders of magnitude different, and it's the private sector that's essentially filling in that funding gap at the moment.
"The government is not a credible investment partner, I think, for industry at this point. I think that that can change, but if you just look at the numbers, they speak for themselves."
Taylor Price warned against forcing frontier AI labs to give local companies free access to computing power.
"You don't want multinationals subsidising Australia. You want open and equitable market positions where Australian companies can thrive," he said. "We do need to find a way that Australian companies get [computing power], but without distorting the market, such that we get unintended consequences."
Industry Minister Tim Ayres and Assistant Technology Minister Andrew Charlton are exploring ways to force AI giants to make their huge data centre capacity available to local start-ups and innovators in a bid to capture a growing share of the global AI supply chain.
Charlton is also on a drive to promote local AI development amid fears the digital economy will be hollowed out by Silicon Valley tech giants.
Taylor Price and Navfield said local businesses and government customers too often defaulted to overseas vendors.
"The demand has assumed that it must be foreign sourced at the moment, so the demand needs to be recentred around Australia first to see if there is a capability, even before we start to look at the assumption that we must go overseas," Navfield said.
Taylor Price said there was an irony to that view. "About 98 per cent of our pipeline is offshore. So the foreign companies think we're able to provide the best service in the world, but the Australian government thinks it has to go to foreign companies ... so there's just a direct contradiction in opinion there."
